steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Key differences between DNA and RNA

Chemical makeup  
• Sugar component  
  – DNA: deoxyribose (lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon).  
  – RNA: ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
• Nitrogenous bases  
  – DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), thymine (T).  
  – RNA: A, G, C, uracil (U) replaces thymine.  
• Strand structure  
  – DNA: usually double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
  – RNA: usually single-stranded; can fold back on itself to form complex 3-D shapes (hairpins, loops).  

Physical properties  
• Stability  
  – DNA is more chemically stable (missing 2′-OH makes it less prone to hydrolysis); suited for long-term genetic storage.  
  – RNA’s extra 2′-OH makes it more reactive and less stable; suited for short-term tasks.  
• Length  
  – Genomic DNA molecules are typically millions of nucleotides long.  
  – RNA molecules are much shorter—anywhere from <100 nt (tRNA) to several thousand nt (mRNA).  

Biological roles  
• DNA  
  – Permanent repository of hereditary information in almost all organisms (some viruses use RNA genomes).  
  – Replicates once per cell cycle; passed to daughter cells.  
• RNA  
  – Messenger RNA (mRNA): carries gene transcripts to ribosomes.  
  – Ribosomal RNA (rRNA): structural & catalytic core of ribosomes.  
  – Transfer RNA (tRNA): delivers amino acids during translation.  
  – Regulatory/enzymatic RNAs: miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA, snRNA, ribozymes, etc.  

Cellular location  
• DNA: mostly confined to nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes); small amounts in mitochondria/chloroplasts.  
• RNA: synthesized in nucleus (or nucleoid) but functions throughout the cell—cytoplasm, ribosomes, organelles.  

Replication & turnover  
• DNA replication: semi-conservative, highly accurate, template-dependent polymerases, proofreading.  
• RNA synthesis (transcription): uses DNA as template, lower fidelity, much higher turnover; many RNAs are degraded minutes to hours after synthesis.  

Functional consequence  
• Because DNA is stable and double-stranded, it excels at long-term information storage and error correction.  
• Because RNA is versatile, single-stranded, and can adopt diverse structures, it acts as a messenger, catalyst, regulator, and— in some viruses—genome.
